Barnard's Unconditional Test for Comparing Two Independent Proportions in a 2 x 2 Table

Source: R/barnardTest.R
barnardTest.Rd

An exact unconditional test for \(2 \times 2\) contingency tables, offering a more powerful alternative to Fisher's exact test by avoiding conditioning on both marginal totals.

Usage

barnardTest(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),
  method = c("csm", "z-pooled", "z-unpooled", "boschloo", "santner-snell"),
  fixed = 1,
  tsMethod = c("square", "central"),
  delta = 0,
  conf.level = NA,
  npNumbers = 100,
  npInterval = FALSE,
  beta = 0.001
)

Arguments

x

a numeric vector or a two-dimensional contingency table in matrix form. x and y can also both be factors.

y

a factor object; ignored if x is a matrix.

alternative

a character string specifying the alternative hypothesis, must be one of "two.sided" (default), "greater" or "less", referring to \(\pi_1 - \pi_2\) relative to delta. You can specify just the initial letter.

method

the ordering of the tables, one of "csm" (default), "z-pooled", "z-unpooled", "boschloo" or "santner-snell". See Details.

fixed

indicates which margin is fixed: 1 for rows (default), 2 for columns, or NA for none of both (multinomial model).

tsMethod

the two-sided method, "square" (default) or "central". See Details.

delta

the difference \(\pi_1 - \pi_2\) under the null hypothesis, strictly between -1 and 1; non-zero values give tests of non-inferiority or superiority. Binomial model only.

conf.level

confidence level of the interval for \(\pi_1 - \pi_2\) (binomial model only). The default NA computes no interval.

npNumbers

the number of grid points for the nuisance parameter, at least 2, default 100.

npInterval

logical, restrict the nuisance parameter to a confidence interval (Berger and Boos, 1994), default FALSE.

beta

the error probability of that interval, default 0.001; only used with npInterval = TRUE.

Value

A list with class "htest" containing the following components:

statistic

the ordering statistic of the observed table: z (z-pooled, z-unpooled), d (Santner-Snell, the difference minus delta) or p.Fisher (Boschloo); absent for CSM, whose ordering has no statistic.

parameter

the sizes n1, n2 of the two samples (binomial model) or the total sample size N (multinomial model).

p.value

the p-value of the test.

conf.int

the confidence interval, if conf.level is not NA.

estimate

the observed difference in proportions (binomial) or in products of proportions (multinomial).

null.value

the difference under the null hypothesis.

alternative

a character string describing the alternative hypothesis.

np

the value(s) of the nuisance parameter(s) that maximize the p-value.

np.range

the range of nuisance parameters considered.

model, tsmethod

the sampling model and the two-sided method.

method

a character string describing the test.

data.name

a character string giving the name of the data.

Details

Two fundamentally different exact tests exist for the equality of two binomial probabilities: Fisher's exact test (Fisher, 1925), which conditions on both margins, and Barnard's unconditional test (Barnard, 1945), which does not. Fisher's test is by far the more widely used, and Fisher himself objected strongly to Barnard's proposal. For 2 x 2 tables, however, Barnard's test is generally more powerful, as Barnard already pointed out; its limited use is mainly due to its computational cost (Mehta and Senchaudhuri, 2003).

Choice of test. In most studies only one margin is fixed by design, e.g. the group sizes of a randomised trial, while the number of events is random. Conditioning on both margins, as Fisher's exact test does, then makes the test markedly conservative: because of the discreteness of the conditional distribution, the actual level often lies far below the nominal one, at the cost of power, in particular for the small samples for which exact tests are used. Unconditional tests avoid this. Boschloo's test, which orders the tables by Fisher's p-value, is uniformly more powerful than Fisher's test: its p-value never exceeds Fisher's, while it still keeps the nominal level (Boschloo, 1970). Lydersen et al. (2009) therefore recommend unconditional tests (or Fisher's mid-p) instead of the traditional Fisher test, and the score statistic ("z-pooled") is to be preferred to the Wald statistic ("z-unpooled"), which can behave poorly (Mehrotra et al., 2003).

For two independent proportions with fixed group sizes, barnardTest() is thus the recommended choice; CSM and Boschloo are the most powerful orderings, z-pooled is the most widely used one. fisher.test() remains appropriate for r x c tables, for exact conditional inference on the odds ratio, when both margins are fixed by design, and whenever conditional inference is wanted on principle: whether the event margin should be conditioned on is a long-standing debate (Yates, 1984; Little, 1989).

Sampling model. Unconditional exact tests can be performed for binomial or multinomial models. The binomial model assumes that the row or the column margins (but not both) are fixed by design, the multinomial model only the total sample size. fixed selects the model: 1 (default) for fixed rows, 2 for fixed columns, NA for the multinomial model. Conditioning on both margins leads to Fisher's exact test, see fisher.test().

Binomial model. The fixed margin defines the two groups, of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\); the first category of the other classification counts the successes \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). The tested difference is \(\pi_1 - \pi_2\) with the estimate \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\), \(\hat{p}_i = x_i/n_i\), against the null value delta. Under the null hypothesis the probability of a table is $$P(x_1, x_2) = \binom{n_1}{x_1}(\pi+\delta)^{x_1}(1-\pi-\delta)^{n_1-x_1} \binom{n_2}{x_2}\pi^{x_2}(1-\pi)^{n_2-x_2},$$ where \(\pi\) is the unknown nuisance parameter. The tables are ordered by how extreme they are, the p-value for a given \(\pi\) is the probability of all tables at least as extreme as the observed one, and the p-value of the test is its maximum over \(\pi\). The maximum is searched on a grid of npNumbers equally spaced values over the admissible range \([\max(0, -\delta), \min(1, 1-\delta)]\), bounds included, and then refined locally with optimize().

method defines the ordering:

"csm"

Barnard's original convexity, symmetry and minimum ordering (CSM; Barnard, 1947). Starting from the most extreme table, the table that increases the maximal p-value least is added to the rejection region, step by step. Generally the most powerful choice; binomial model only.

"z-pooled"

the score statistic $$Z = \frac{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2-\delta}{\sqrt{\tilde{p}_1(1-\tilde{p}_1)/n_1 + \tilde{p}_2(1-\tilde{p}_2)/n_2}},$$ with the pooled proportion for \(\tilde{p}_1 = \tilde{p}_2\) if \(\delta = 0\), and the restricted maximum likelihood estimates (Miettinen and Nurminen, 1985) otherwise (Suissa and Shuster, 1985).

"z-unpooled"

the Wald statistic, with the unrestricted estimates \(\hat{p}_i\) in the variance (and the same numerator \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2-\delta\)).

"boschloo"

the p-value of Fisher's exact test (Boschloo, 1970).

"santner-snell"

the plain difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) (Santner and Snell, 1980).

Two-sided tests are by default based on the absolute value of the statistic, i.e. on a region that is symmetric about the null value (tsMethod = "square"). With tsMethod = "central" the two-sided p-value is twice the smaller one-sided p-value.

With npInterval = TRUE the maximum is only searched within a \(100(1-\beta)\)% Clopper-Pearson interval of the nuisance parameter and \(\beta\) is added to the p-value (Berger and Boos, 1994). The interval is based on the pooled successes, which are binomial only for \(\delta = 0\); it is therefore not available with a non-zero delta, a confidence interval or CSM.

The confidence interval for \(\pi_1 - \pi_2\) (binomial model only) is computed if conf.level is not NA, and is obtained by inverting the test over delta. It is computationally demanding, in particular for CSM, where the ordering has to be rebuilt for every candidate value.

Multinomial model. Only the total \(N\) is fixed. The nuisance parameters are the probabilities of the first row and of the first column, and the tested quantity is the difference in the products of the cell proportions, \((x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21})/N^2\). Available for the z-pooled, z-unpooled and Boschloo orderings, with delta = 0 and without confidence interval.

If x is a matrix, it is taken as a two-dimensional contingency table, and hence its entries should be nonnegative integers. Otherwise, both x and y must be vectors of the same length. Incomplete cases are removed, the vectors are coerced into factor objects, and the contingency table is computed from these.

Note

The algorithms follow the Exact package by Peter Calhoun (Exact::exact.test()), with these deliberate differences:

  • the rejection region of the ordering statistics consists of exactly the tables that are at least as extreme as the observed one. Exact builds it by walking the boundary and filling rows and columns by convexity, which in two-sided tests can admit tables that are less extreme (e.g. matrix(c(3, 2, 1, 0), 2), z-pooled: 0.783 instead of 0.568);

  • the nuisance grid includes the bounds of the admissible range (Exact uses 0.00001 and 0.99999), where the maximum can lie;

  • the z-unpooled statistic subtracts delta in the numerator, as the z-pooled one does;

  • the stored CSM orderings of the companion package ExactData are not used: the compiled ordering is fast enough to be computed on the fly, for every npNumbers;

  • when the grid maximum is attained at several nuisance values, the refined p-value is the largest of the refined maxima (Exact takes the smallest).

References

Barnard, G.A. (1947) Significance tests for 2x2 tables. Biometrika, 34:123-138.

Berger, R.L. and Boos, D.D. (1994) P values maximised over a confidence set for the nuisance parameter. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 89:1012-1016.

Boschloo, R.D. (1970) Raised conditional level of significance for the 2x2-table when testing the equality of two probabilities. Statistica Neerlandica, 24:1-35.

Calhoun, P. (2024) Exact: Unconditional Exact Test. R package version 3.3.

Little, R.J.A. (1989) Testing the equality of two independent binomial proportions. The American Statistician, 43:283-288.

Lydersen, S., Fagerland, M.W. and Laake, P. (2009) Recommended tests for association in 2x2 tables. Statistics in Medicine, 28:1159-1175.

Mehrotra, D.V., Chan, I.S.F. and Berger, R.L. (2003) A cautionary note on exact unconditional inference for a difference between two independent binomial proportions. Biometrics, 59:441-450.

Mehta, C.R., Senchaudhuri, P. (2003) Conditional versus unconditional exact tests for comparing two binomials. Cytel Software Corporation, technical report.

Miettinen, O. and Nurminen, M. (1985) Comparative analysis of two rates. Statistics in Medicine, 4:213-226.

Examples

tab <- as.table(matrix(c(8, 14, 1, 3), nrow=2,
                dimnames=list(treat=c("I","II"), out=c("I","II"))))
barnardTest(tab, method="z-pooled")
#> 
#> 	Barnard's unconditional exact test (z-pooled ordering)
#> 
#> data:  tab
#> z = 0.43944, n1 = 9, n2 = 17, p-value = 0.7858
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in proportion is not equal to 0
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in proportion 
#>               0.06535948 
#> 

# the default CSM ordering
barnardTest(tab)
#> 
#> 	Barnard's unconditional exact test (CSM ordering)
#> 
#> data:  tab
#> n1 = 9, n2 = 17, p-value = 0.7181
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in proportion is not equal to 0
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in proportion 
#>               0.06535948 
#> 

# Mehta and Senchaudhuri (2003), vaccine example
tab <- as.table(matrix(c(7, 12, 8, 3), nrow=2,
                       dimnames=list(treat=c("vaccine","placebo"),
                                     infection=c("yes","no"))))
barnardTest(tab, alternative="less")
#> 
#> 	Barnard's unconditional exact test (CSM ordering)
#> 
#> data:  tab
#> n1 = 15, n2 = 15, p-value = 0.03669
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in proportion is less than 0
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in proportion 
#>               -0.3333333 
#> 

# non-inferiority margin of -0.1, with confidence interval
barnardTest(tab, method="z-pooled", alternative="greater", delta=-0.1,
            conf.level=0.95)
#> 
#> 	Barnard's unconditional exact test (z-pooled ordering)
#> 
#> data:  tab
#> z = -1.339, n1 = 15, n2 = 15, p-value = 0.9444
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in proportion is greater than -0.1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  -0.5963737  1.0000000
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in proportion 
#>               -0.3333333 
#> 

# multinomial model: only the total is fixed
barnardTest(tab, method="boschloo", fixed=NA)
#> 
#> 	Barnard's unconditional exact test (Boschloo ordering)
#> 
#> data:  tab
#> p.Fisher = 0.12814, N = 30, p-value = 0.08367
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in product of proportion is not equal to 0
#> sample estimates:
#> difference in product of proportion 
#>                         -0.08333333 
#>
